title: First strategy: read the hand, not the last win
subtitle: 2 introductions · 5 practice · 5 independent tasks

theory.text: Use your current hand and the dealer upcard, not the previous round's win or loss. In our 6D/S17/DAS/late-surrender/peek/3:2 profile, hard 5–8 always Hit; hard 17–20 Stand. These boundaries remain the same against a small card or an ace. For example, 3+5 against 6 needs Hit, but 10+7 against 10 needs Stand. A strong dealer card does not mean you should always draw, and a good action can still lose. This first lesson focuses on hard hands without a splittable pair; soft hands, doubles and pairs follow separately. Try two guided examples, then ten scored decisions. Correct a mistake to continue, but the first answer remains the score.

coaching.explanation: Hard 8 against 6. With 5–8, Hit against any upcard: this hand needs improvement.
coaching.contrast: Compare 3+5 against 10 → Hit with 10+7 against 10 → Stand: the dealer is unchanged, but your total crosses the boundary.

mistakes.hit: Being allowed to draw does not make it best. Compare your total and the dealer boundary.
mistakes.stand: Standing does not improve this hand. Check whether Hit or an available Double is required; ignore the previous outcome.
mistakes.doubleDown: Not every small total calls for Double: it needs the right upcard and a two-card hand.

theory.text: Keep the hand fixed and change only the dealer upcard. It often changes the best action, but the groups are not absolute. With hard 12, Stand against 4–6; Hit against 2–3 and 7–A. With hard 13–14, Stand against 2–6 and Hit against 7–A. Hard 8 still Hits a small card, while hard 17 still Stands against an ace. Compare 10+2 against 3 (Hit) and against 4 (Stand). Do not imagine that the dealer's hidden card is always ten; this is a reference strategy for the stated six-deck rules, not a prediction of one round. Practise recognizing the boundary before memorizing more totals.

theory.text: Double takes exactly one more card and ends the hand, so a small total alone is not enough. In our six-deck S17 profile, hard 9 doubles against 3–6; hard 10 against 2–9; hard 11 against 2–10, but Hits against an ace. Outside each range choose Hit. Double is available only on the first two cards here: after an extra card, the fallback for hard 9–11 is Hit, not Stand. Compare 5+6 against 6 (Double), 5+6 against A (Hit), and 2+3+6 against 6 (Hit because Double is unavailable). Follow the dealer boundary and the actual controls; do not transfer these rules automatically to H17 or another profile.
